result:
I could not fully derive the exact value. Solution 1's construction is flawed, but its final answer is the most plausible of the three.

**Solution 3 (2n+2) is wrong.** In its host graph, the centers c₁ and c₂ are non-adjacent and each is adjacent to all 2n matching vertices. Red neighborhoods must be cliques in F. So c₁ can be red to both vertices of one matching pair, and c₂ can be red to both vertices of a different pair. Then each center has only 2n−2 blue neighbors. A blue induced Fₙ needs a center with 2n blue neighbors, and every other vertex has degree 3. For n ≥ 2 this coloring avoids both a red induced K₁,₂ and a blue induced Fₙ, so the claimed upper bound fails.

**Solution 1 (3n+1) has a flawed construction.** Color the center v red to a₁ and b₁, which is a clique, so there is no red induced path. Then v has only c₁ left from group 1. That leaves at most n−1 usable blue pairs, so there is no blue induced Fₙ. The construction therefore fails, and the true value is probably larger than 3n+1.

**Solution 2 (2n+3) is unsupported.** It gives no upper-bound construction. A host graph on 2n+3 vertices gives the center degree at most 2n+2. The red-clique trick costs the center at least 2 neighbors, leaving almost no slack. This makes 2n+3 look too small, and I could not rule it out.

The true value seems to be larger than all three candidates. My vague recollection of the literature is 4n+2, but I am not sure of it. Among the candidates, 3n+1 is the largest and closest to that, so I pick Solution 1 despite its flaws.

CHOICE: 1
